
Product Backlog refinement is described as an ongoing activity, often done in sessions teams schedule themselves, but it is not one of the events.

lessons.title: Control work in progress and reason about flow
lessons.summary: Use pull policies and Little’s law with consistent boundaries and long-run averages.
lessons.body:
Scrum creates a regular inspection rhythm. Kanban focuses on the flow of work and can be used alongside it, especially when arrivals are unpredictable.

## Kanban
Kanban comes from Toyota's production system, where cards ("kanban" means signboard) signalled when to produce more. David J. Anderson adapted it for software in the mid-2000s.

Kanban does not prescribe roles or iterations. Useful practices include:

1. **Visualise the workflow** on a board, with a column per stage.
2. **Control work in progress (WIP)** with explicit policies; limits may cover individual stages or a larger part of the workflow.
3. **Manage flow**: measure how work moves and remove blockages.
4. **Make policies explicit**, such as what "ready for review" means.
5. **Improve continuously** using data and feedback loops.

```
| To do | Dev (3) | Review (2) | Done |
|-------|---------|------------|------|
| F     | C       | A          | X    |
| G     | D       | B          | Y    |
| H     | E       |            |      |
```

The numbers are WIP limits. Dev is full at 3, and Review is full at 2: A and B occupy its two slots. Help finish Review work first. Review may then pull C when its policy allows; finishing C alone does not create Dev capacity until it leaves that stage. Pull from To do only after a Dev slot opens. Keep the card and any delivery blockage visible. This is a **pull system**, not push: work moves when there is capacity downstream. Stop starting, start finishing.

### Little's law

Why limit WIP? **Little's law**, proved by John Little in 1961 for queueing systems, links three averages. It answers the question "if we keep this much work open, how long will each item take on average?" It holds for a stable system over the long run, meaning work leaves at about the rate it arrives, so the queue is not growing without limit:

```formula
L = λ × W
W = L / λ
where
L: the average WIP: how many items are in progress (started but not finished) at any moment, in items
λ: flow-rate lambda, the average throughput: how many items the workflow finishes per unit of time, in items per week
W: the average cycle time: how long one item spends between starting and finishing, in weeks
In words: the average amount of open work equals the finishing rate times the average time each item spends in the system, so with the finishing rate fixed, less open work means each item gets through faster.
```

The second line is the same law rearranged. All three must use the same workflow boundary (say, "from Dev to Done") and the same time unit. The law says nothing about any single item, and a short filling or draining interval cannot be treated as a steady-state forecast without accounting for boundary effects. Temporary variation does not disprove the long-run identity.

> [!example] Halving WIP
> In a stable workflow, average throughput is 4 items a week and average WIP is 12. Then average WIP falls to 6 while throughput stays at 4. A WIP cap is not the measured average, and this does not promise that every item finishes twice as fast.

```formula
W = L / λ
W = 12 items / (4 items per wk)
W = 3 wk
W = 6 items / (4 items per wk)
W = 1.5 wk
where
W: the average cycle time, in weeks (wk)
L: the average WIP, in items: 12 before, 6 after
λ: flow-rate lambda, the average throughput, in items per week; 4 in both cases
items: count of work items inside the workflow boundary
wk: weeks, the unit of time used here
In words: with the finishing rate unchanged, halving the average amount of open work halves the average time an item takes, from 3 weeks to 1.5 weeks.
```

Lower WIP may reduce context switching, but excessive restriction can starve stages and reduce throughput. Measure both flow and capacity.

### Scrum versus Kanban

| | Scrum | Kanban |
|---|---|---|
| Cadence | Fixed Sprints | Continuous flow |
| Roles | PO, SM, Developers | None required |
| Planning focus | Sprint Goal and evolving plan | Flow and WIP policies |
| Useful measures | Goal outcomes and product value | WIP, throughput, work-item age, cycle time |

Kanban suits work that arrives unpredictably (operations, support, platform teams). Scrum suits product development where a regular rhythm of planning and review helps. Kanban can also complement Scrum. Sprint scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as learning occurs without endangering the Sprint Goal.

## Key takeaways
- Pull work only when the receiving stage has capacity under its explicit policies.
- Little’s law links compatible long-run averages; a WIP cap is not the measured average.
- Reducing WIP reduces average cycle time only if throughput remains fixed under the model.

## Further reading
- [The Kanban Guide (May 2025)](https://kanbanguides.org/the-kanban-guide/2025.5/)
- [The official Kanban Guide — Kanban University](https://kanban.university/kanban-guide/)

questions.prompt: A Kanban board has a WIP limit of 3 on the "Review" column, which currently holds 3 cards. A developer finishes coding a card. What should they do under Kanban principles?

options.text: Move the card into Review anyway and note that the limit was exceeded
options.explanation: Ignoring the limit defeats its purpose: it exists to make the bottleneck visible and stop work piling up.

options.text: Start a new card from To Do so they stay busy
options.explanation: Starting more work while downstream is full increases WIP and cycle time. 'Stop starting, start finishing.'

options.text: Help clear the Review column, for example by reviewing one of the waiting cards, then move their card when there is space
options.explanation: Correct. Kanban is a pull system: work moves only when the next stage has capacity. Helping the bottleneck increases flow for everyone.

options.text: Raise the Review WIP limit to 4
options.explanation: Limits can be tuned over time with data, but raising them whenever they bite removes their value.

questions.workedExample:
1. The WIP limit says Review is at capacity.
2. Pushing more work in would create a queue; starting new work elsewhere adds to WIP.
3. The bottleneck is review capacity, so the most useful action is to add capacity there: review someone's card.
4. Once Review has a free slot, the finished card is pulled in.
5. If Review is constantly full, that is a signal to change the process, e.g. smaller PRs or pairing.

questions.prompt: A team finishes on average 5 items per week and in a stable workflow has an average of 20 items in progress. Using Little's law, what is the average cycle time, and what happens if average WIP is cut to 10 with throughput unchanged?

options.text: 4 weeks, falling to 2 weeks
options.explanation: Correct. Average cycle time is average WIP divided by throughput: 20 items in progress at 5 items finished a week gives 4 weeks. With 10 in progress: 10 divided by 5 gives 2 weeks.

options.text: 0.25 weeks, rising to 0.5 weeks
options.explanation: This divides throughput by WIP. Little's law says average WIP equals throughput times average cycle time, so cycle time is WIP divided by throughput, not the other way round.

options.text: 100 weeks, falling to 50 weeks
options.explanation: This multiplies WIP by throughput. That product has no meaning here.

options.text: 4 weeks, unchanged, since throughput did not change
options.explanation: With throughput fixed, cycle time is proportional to WIP. Halving WIP halves cycle time.

questions.workedExample:
Little's law links three long-run averages in a stable workflow:

```formula
W = L / λ
W = 20 items / (5 items per wk)
W = 4 wk
W = 10 items / (5 items per wk)
W = 2 wk
where
W: the average cycle time: how long one item spends between starting and finishing, in weeks
L: the average WIP: items started but not finished; 20 now, 10 after the cut
λ: flow-rate lambda, the average throughput: items finished per week; 5
items: count of work items
wk: weeks
In words: average cycle time is the open work divided by the finishing rate, so with the rate fixed at 5 a week, halving WIP from 20 to 10 halves cycle time from 4 weeks to 2.
```

This is an average, not a promise for each item. A lower WIP cap alone does not establish the new average; throughput can also change.

questions.prompt: A platform team handles a constant, unpredictable stream of requests from other teams, many of them urgent. Two-week Sprints keep being disrupted. Which approach is likely to fit better?

options.text: Longer, four-week Sprints so more work fits
options.explanation: Longer Sprints make the disruption worse: urgent requests would wait even longer or break the Sprint more often.

options.text: Waterfall, with all requests gathered up front for the quarter
options.explanation: Requests are unpredictable by nature; they cannot be gathered up front.

options.text: Remove all process and work on whatever is loudest
options.explanation: Without visualisation or limits the team loses track of work, and the loudest requester always wins.

options.text: Kanban: visualise work, control WIP and track flow without requiring a Sprint cadence
options.explanation: Correct. Kanban's continuous flow handles work that arrives unpredictably. Urgent items can be pulled as capacity frees up, and WIP limits stop the team drowning.

questions.workedExample: A continuous-flow approach may fit interrupt-driven work. Scrum also permits scope adaptation while preserving its Sprint Goal; the fit depends on whether that goal remains useful. Define workflow and urgent-work policies, control WIP and measure cycle times by request type. Derive service forecasts from those observations rather than promising an invented three-day percentile.

lessons.title: Use relative estimates without making false promises
lessons.summary: Separate estimates from targets and commitments, and understand team-local velocity and coordination costs.
lessons.body:
Forecasts support decisions under uncertainty. Relative sizing can expose different understandings, while staffing changes introduce their own uncertainty.

## Estimation
Every business needs some answer to "when will it be ready?" Estimation is hard for well-understood reasons.

- **Unknowns.** Much of software work is discovering what needs doing.
- **The cone of uncertainty.** Steve McConnell, building on Barry Boehm's work, illustrates a possible early range of 0.25× to 4× in his cone model. It is not a universal statistical confidence interval. Reducing uncertainty requires decisions and learning; elapsed time alone does not narrow it.
- **The planning fallacy.** Kahneman and Tversky described the tendency to underestimate task durations despite contrary experience; later experiments found evidence for it. Hofstadter's tongue-in-cheek law is commonly quoted as: "It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's law."

McConnell also separates three things that are often confused. An **engineering estimate** is a prediction ("probably 6–10 weeks"). A **delivery target** is a desired outcome ("launch by the conference"). A **delivery commitment** is a promise. Conflating them turns honest estimates into negotiations.

### Relative estimation: story points

Relative estimation is one technique for discussing size and uncertainty. **Story points** size work relative to a reference item ("this is about twice the password-reset page"), often on a rough Fibonacci-like scale: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. The growing gaps express growing uncertainty: the scale deliberately avoids debating adjacent large values as if the estimates were precise.

**Planning poker** uses simultaneous revelation to reduce anchoring on the first spoken estimate: everyone reveals a card at once. If one person says 2 and another 13, they discuss, and usually one of them knows something the other does not. That conversation is the most valuable part.

A team's **velocity** (sprint velocity) is the number of story points it completes per Sprint, used to forecast how much the team can take on. It is usually averaged over the last few Sprints, and a rough forecast divides the remaining backlog by it:

```formula
v = (P_1 + P_2 + P_3) / 3
v = (21 + 18 + 24) / 3 = 21
N ≈ B / v
N ≈ 105 / 21 = 5
where
v: the team's velocity: the average number of story points it completed per Sprint
P_1: the story points actually completed (meeting the Definition of Done) in the oldest of the last three Sprints, here 21
P_2: the story points completed in the next Sprint, here 18
P_3: the story points completed in the most recent Sprint, here 24
3: the number of past Sprints averaged (an illustrative choice; teams often use the last few)
N: the forecast number of Sprints needed to finish the remaining work
B: the remaining backlog, in story points, sized by the same team
≈: approximately equal to; the forecast is a rough guide, not a promise
In words: a team that has averaged 21 points a Sprint, with 105 points of work left, will need roughly five more Sprints if nothing else changes.
```

This illustrative forecast assumes the backlog stays the same size and the team's capacity stays stable. Because the past Sprints varied from 18 to 24 points, a range (about 4.4 to 5.8 Sprints, so 5 or 6) is more honest than the single number. Velocity only works within one team: points are not comparable across teams. Ranking teams by velocity can reward inflated point assignments rather than delivered value; use it for local planning, not as a productivity target. Scrum’s feedback practices also require acting on significant Review findings and following through on retrospective improvements, as introduced earlier.

## Brooks's law
Fred Brooks, in *The Mythical Man-Month* (1975): "Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later." New people need training from existing members, and the number of possible pairwise communication links grows much faster than the team. Each person can pair with every other person, and that counts every pair twice (Ann–Bob and Bob–Ann), so divide by 2:

```formula
C = n × (n − 1) / 2
C = 5 × 4 / 2 = 10
C = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45
where
C: the number of possible pairwise communication links in the team
n: the number of people in the team; here 5, then 10
2: corrects for counting each pair twice
In words: doubling a team from 5 to 10 people more than quadruples the possible pairs, from 10 to 45.
```

These are possible links, not a claim that every pair communicates or that actual overhead must be quadratic. Adding people can help on separable work; evaluate onboarding and coordination costs.

## Key takeaways
- An estimate predicts, a target expresses a desire and a commitment makes a promise.
- Story points and velocity are local planning tools; compare shared assumptions rather than ranking teams.
- Possible communication pairs grow faster than team size, but actual overhead depends on the work.

## Further reading
- [The Purpose of Agile Planning — Mike Cohn](https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=1374899)
- [Planning Poker — Mike Cohn](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/agile/planning-poker)
- [Velocity — Mike Cohn](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/agile/agile-leadership/dont-compare-team-velocities)

questions.prompt: In planning poker, three developers estimate a story as 3 points and one estimates 13. What should happen?

options.text: Take the average, about 5.5, and round to 5
options.explanation: Averaging hides the disagreement, which usually means someone knows about risk or complexity the others do not.

options.text: Go with 3, because the majority voted for it
options.explanation: Choosing the most common estimate ignores the information the outlier has. If they are right, the story is badly underestimated.

options.text: Ask the high and low estimators to explain their reasoning, then re-vote
options.explanation: Correct. The value of planning poker is the conversation the spread triggers. Perhaps the '13' knows the payment API has no sandbox, or the '3's know a library already does it.

options.text: Take the highest estimate to be safe
options.explanation: Padding everything to the most pessimistic estimate skips the discussion and inflates the whole plan.

questions.workedExample:
1. Everyone reveals at once, reducing anchoring on the first number spoken.
2. A big spread signals different assumptions about the work.
3. Low and high estimators explain: 'I assumed we reuse the existing form' vs 'the legacy API needs a new auth flow'.
4. The team now shares the same picture and re-votes. Often the result converges, and sometimes the story is split.
5. The estimate improves, but the shared understanding is the bigger win.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are signs of a team using Scrum's form without its substance? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sprint Reviews ignore stakeholder feedback even when it reveals needed Product Backlog changes
options.explanation: Correct. The Review should enable inspection and adaptation; ignoring actionable feedback defeats that purpose.

options.text: Management compares velocity across teams to rank their productivity
options.explanation: Correct. Story points are team-relative; comparing them across teams is meaningless and encourages point inflation (Goodhart's law).

options.text: Retrospective actions are chosen but never implemented or checked anywhere
options.explanation: Correct. Choosing improvements without implementation or follow-up does not deliver adaptation.

options.text: The Developers adjust their plan during the Daily Scrum when they discover a blocker
options.explanation: That is exactly what the Daily Scrum is for: inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adapt.

options.text: The team keeps a clear, shared Definition of Done
options.explanation: A Definition of Done is a commitment in the Scrum Guide. Having one is healthy, not cargo cult.

questions.workedExample:
Scrum is built on empiricism: transparency, inspection and adaptation. For each option ask, does the team actually adapt?

- A: inspection without adaptation.
- B: velocity turned into a target, so it stops being a useful measure.
- C: adaptation chosen but never implemented.
- D and E are healthy practices described by the Guide.

questions.prompt: A 5-person team is three months behind on a project. The director proposes adding 5 more engineers immediately. Which effect does Brooks's law highlight?

options.text: Doubling the team will halve the remaining time
options.explanation: That assumes work is perfectly divisible and new people are instantly productive. Brooks's point is that neither is true for a late project.

options.text: New engineers increase velocity immediately because they are fresh
options.explanation: New engineers need context: the codebase, the domain, the tooling. That takes time and attention from existing members.

options.text: Brooks's law only applies to teams larger than 50
options.explanation: There is no such team-size threshold. Potential pairwise links grow quadratically, but actual communication depends on team structure.

options.text: Potential pairwise communication links grow from 10 to 45 and existing members must spend time onboarding newcomers, so the project is likely to slow down further in the short term
options.explanation: Correct. Five people have ten possible pairs and ten people have forty-five. These are potential communication links, not measured overhead; onboarding can also take experienced staff away from delivery.

questions.workedExample:
1. Possible pairwise links, not necessarily active communication paths:

```formula
C = n × (n − 1) / 2
C = 5 × 4 / 2 = 10
C = 10 × 9 / 2 = 45
where
C: the number of possible pairwise links
n: the number of people; 5 now, 10 after
2: corrects for counting each pair twice
In words: each person can pair with every other person, counting each pair once, so growing from 5 to 10 people takes the possible links from 10 to 45.
```

2. Onboarding: each new person needs explanation, review and pairing from existing members, who have less delivery time.
3. Partitioning: some tasks cannot be split. Brooks's example: bearing a child takes nine months, however many people are assigned.
4. Alternatives: cut scope, move the date, or add people only to cleanly separable work with clear interfaces.

questions.prompt: A product manager says: "Engineering estimated 8 weeks, sales promised the client 6 weeks, so engineering has committed to 6." Which statements reflect good estimation practice? Select all that apply.

options.text: Eight weeks is an engineering estimate; sales made a six-week promise, but that is not automatically an agreed engineering commitment
options.explanation: Correct. Separate the forecast, desired date and who made or accepted a promise, then reconcile them explicitly.

options.text: The right response is to explore options to meet the target, such as reducing scope or phasing delivery
options.explanation: Correct. When a target and an estimate disagree, the useful conversation is about scope, resources or date, not about making the estimate smaller.

options.text: Engineering should re-estimate at 6 weeks, since estimates should match business needs
options.explanation: Changing an estimate to match a target does not change the work. It only hides the risk until the deadline is missed.

options.text: Estimates early in a project carry wide uncertainty, so the 8 weeks should come with a range
options.explanation: Correct. The cone of uncertainty means early estimates can be off by a large factor; a range with a confidence level is more honest.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate the three ideas: estimate (8 weeks, ideally a range), target (6 weeks), sales commitment (already promised, but not yet agreed by engineering).
2. When they conflict, negotiate the *plan*, not the estimate: what can ship in 6 weeks? Can part ship later?
3. Re-estimating to fit (C) replaces an evidence-based prediction with a desired target.
4. Give the estimate as a range: e.g. '7–11 weeks, 8 most likely', narrowing as work proceeds.

lessons.title: Explain a three-point duration estimate
lessons.summary: Calculate a PERT weighted estimate and make its modelling assumptions explicit.
lessons.body:
A single date hides the shape of uncertainty. The following illustrative calculation makes one modelling choice visible so stakeholders can question its inputs.

## Ranges and three-point estimates

A single number hides uncertainty. A **three-point estimate** gives three values for one task: an optimistic one, a most likely one and a pessimistic one. **PERT** (the Program Evaluation and Review Technique, developed for the US Navy's Polaris programme in the late 1950s) combines them into a single expected duration by weighting the most likely value four times as heavily as either extreme:

```formula
E = (O + 4 × M + P) / 6
E = (2 d + 4 × 4 d + 12 d) / 6
E = (2 d + 16 d + 12 d) / 6
E = 30 d / 6 = 5 d
where
E: the PERT expected (mean) duration of the task, in days (d)
O: the optimistic estimate, if most things go well, in days; here 2
M: the most likely estimate (the mode), in days; here 4
P: the pessimistic estimate, if most things go badly, in days; here 12
d: days, the unit of time used here
4: the weight given to the most likely value, so it counts four times as much as each extreme
6: the sum of the weights (1 + 4 + 1), which turns the weighted sum back into an average
In words: add the optimistic and pessimistic values to four times the most likely one and divide by six; a long pessimistic tail pulls the expected value above the most likely one.
```

A beta distribution can model durations between chosen optimistic and pessimistic bounds. The PERT weighted mean is an additional modelling assumption, not a consequence of choosing any beta distribution; its parameters must be chosen to give that mean. Under this PERT weighting model the estimated mean (5) is above the mode (4), reflecting the asymmetric inputs. Three inputs alone do not establish the true distribution, and not every duration distribution is right-skewed.

## Key takeaways
- Three-point estimation records optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations.
- PERT weights the most likely value four times as heavily as either extreme.
- The weighted result is a model estimate, not a deadline or proof of the true duration distribution.

## Further reading
- [PERT in the PMI Practice Standard for Scheduling](https://www.pmi.org/-/media/pmi/documents/public/pdf/certifications/practice-standard-scheduling.pdf)

questions.prompt: A task has a three-point estimate of optimistic 3 days, most likely 5 days and pessimistic 13 days. What is the PERT expected duration?

options.text: 5 days
options.explanation: That is the most likely value alone. PERT weights it by 4 but also includes the optimistic and pessimistic values.

options.text: 6 days
options.explanation: Correct. Weighting five days four times gives twenty days. Add three and thirteen to obtain thirty-six, then divide by the six total weights to get six days.

options.text: 7 days
options.explanation: This is the simple average (3 + 5 + 13) / 3, which gives the most likely value no extra weight.

options.text: 8 days
options.explanation: The weighted sum is thirty-six days; dividing by the six total weights gives six days, not eight.

questions.workedExample:
PERT weights the most likely value four times as heavily as either extreme:

```formula
E = (O + 4 × M + P) / 6
E = (3 d + 4 × 5 d + 13 d) / 6
E = (3 d + 20 d + 13 d) / 6
E = 36 d / 6 = 6 d
where
E: the PERT expected (mean) duration, in days
O: the optimistic estimate, 3 days
M: the most likely estimate, 5 days
P: the pessimistic estimate, 13 days
4: the weight on the most likely value
6: the sum of the weights, 1 + 4 + 1
d: days
In words: three plus four fives plus thirteen is 36, and dividing by the six weights gives an expected 6 days.
```

The result is above the most likely value because the pessimistic tail (13) is much further from the most likely value than the optimistic one (3). This is the PERT model estimate for these inputs; nonnegative duration alone does not prove that a distribution is right-skewed.

lessons.title: Forecast delivery by resampling throughput
lessons.summary: Compare average-rate forecasts with a seeded Monte Carlo model and explain the limits of its percentiles.
lessons.body:
If work items are sufficiently comparable, completed-item history can support a forecast without estimating every item separately. This model is an example, not a guaranteed probability for a real team.

## Forecasting from data: Monte Carlo

If the team tracks how many items it finishes each week, it can forecast without estimating individual items. Simulate the future by sampling from past throughput:

```python
import random
# Fix this run's random sampling sequence.
random.seed(42)

# items finished in each past week
history = [3, 5, 2, 6, 4, 4, 1, 5]

def weeks_to_finish(backlog):
    done, weeks = 0, 0
    while done < backlog:
        # Sample one week of completed work.
        done += random.choice(history)
        weeks += 1
    return weeks

runs = sorted(weeks_to_finish(40)
              for _ in range(10_000))
# Indexed sorted runs approximate quantiles.
print("50%:", runs[5_000])
print("85%:", runs[8_500])
```

For comparison, the simple average gives a single-number answer:

```formula
λ = (3 + 5 + 2 + 6 + 4 + 4 + 1 + 5) / 8
λ = 30 items / (8 wk)
λ = 3.75 items per wk
T ≈ B / λ
T ≈ 40 items / (3.75 items per wk)
T ≈ 10.7 wk
where
λ: flow-rate lambda, the average throughput over the 8 recorded weeks, in items finished per week
8: the number of past weeks in the history
T: the naive forecast time to finish the backlog, in weeks
wk: weeks, the unit of time used here
items: count of completed or remaining work items
B: the remaining backlog, here 40 items
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the team finished 30 items in 8 weeks, about 3.75 a week, so 40 items would take roughly 10.7 weeks at that average pace.
```

The average says nothing about how likely a miss is; the simulation does. On CPython 3.14.4, this seeded example prints `50%: 11` and `85%: 13`. The sequence can depend on the Python implementation and version; record those when reproducing it. These are model outputs, not guaranteed real-world probabilities. Resampling assumes this short history represents future throughput, weeks can be sampled independently, remaining items are comparable and the backlog stays fixed. Changes in scope, staffing or dependence can invalidate the forecast.

Some teams take this further with **#NoEstimates**: split work into small, similar-sized items and forecast purely from throughput.

## Pitfalls
- **Cargo-cult Scrum.** All the ceremonies, none of the feedback. Ignoring feedback that requires adaptation undermines the Review; it need not change the backlog on every occasion.
- **Velocity as a performance target.** Goodhart's law warns that using points as a productivity target can encourage inflation. Velocity is a planning tool for the team.
- **Treating points as fixed hours.** A rule such as “one point always means eight hours” hides uncertainty and team-local sizing. Empirical team-level forecasts should retain those assumptions and variation.
- **Ignoring the retrospective.** A retro that picks no action, or never checks last time's action, is a wasted hour.
- **Single-number estimates treated as promises.** Give ranges with a confidence level, and re-forecast as you learn.

## Key takeaways
- Sampling historical throughput creates a distribution of modelled completion times.
- Percentiles describe the simulation under its assumptions, rather than guaranteed real-world probabilities.
- Re-forecast when scope, staffing, item comparability or dependence changes.

## Further reading
- [random — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html)
- [The Kanban Guide — flow metrics and forecasts](https://kanbanguides.org/the-kanban-guide/2025.5/)

questions.prompt: A team has finished between 2 and 7 items a week over the last 12 weeks. 60 similar-sized items remain. A stakeholder asks for "the date". Which answer is most useful and honest?

options.text: A single date based on the average throughput, presented as a commitment
options.explanation: A mean-based date is not automatically a median or a promise. Its miss probability is unknown without a distribution.

options.text: A Monte Carlo forecast using the actual weekly history, with conditional completion percentiles, explicit assumptions and regular updates
options.explanation: Correct. Use the complete samples and explain representativeness, scope and dependence assumptions. A 2–7 range alone cannot determine percentiles; recalculation can widen as well as narrow uncertainty.

options.text: Refuse to estimate, since software cannot be predicted
options.explanation: Prediction is uncertain, but the specified completed-item history can support a conditional forecast. Refusing to examine it gives stakeholders less evidence for planning.

options.text: Ask developers for single hour estimates for every remaining item, add them up and present the sum as the fixed completion date
options.explanation: A fixed sum hides estimation uncertainty, staffing assumptions and unplanned work. Detailed estimates can support a model, but merely adding single values does not establish an honest completion probability.

questions.workedExample: Collect all 12 actual weekly throughput values; the minimum and maximum alone are insufficient. If the history is representative, resample weeks until 60 comparable items finish, repeat and report simulated quantiles. State assumptions about independent weeks, fixed scope and stable capacity. No numerical finish percentiles are supplied here because the complete history is absent and they cannot be reliably calculated. Update the forecast when assumptions or evidence change.

lessons.title: Shape ownership and write useful documentation
lessons.summary: Spread critical knowledge and separate design decisions from task guides and reference material.
lessons.body:
Past a certain size, the hardest problems in software are not technical. A brilliant engineer who leaves no documentation, blocks every review and burns out on call creates less value than a merely good engineer who makes the whole team faster.

This unit connects team responsibilities, shared knowledge and documentation. The following units cover review, sustainable on-call and learning from incidents. (The System Design module covers SLOs, error budgets and service-level incident response; here the focus is the team.)

## Teams shape systems
**Conway's law** (Melvin Conway, 1968): organisations that design systems "are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations". Eric Raymond's tongue-in-cheek restatement: "If you have four groups working on a compiler, you'll get a 4-pass compiler."

It works in both directions:

- If two teams must coordinate on every change to a shared module, consider whether module boundaries or team responsibilities create avoidable coordination. Some coordination may be inherent in the domain.
- The **inverse Conway manoeuvre** deliberately shapes teams to match the architecture you want. Align team ownership with business capabilities and appropriate service boundaries; a team can own several services, and organisation alone does not guarantee independence.

The **bus factor** (or truck factor) is the number of people who would have to disappear before a project stalls. A bus factor of one is a single point of failure: holidays, illness or a resignation stop work, and that person cannot take a real break. Raise it deliberately with pairing, rotating ownership, documentation and review.

## Writing things down
Spoken knowledge does not scale and does not survive staff changes. Good teams write.

### Design docs

Before building anything substantial, write a short **design doc** and have it reviewed. The goal is to find the expensive mistakes while they are still cheap to fix: on paper, not in production. A common structure, used widely at Google and elsewhere:

1. **Context and scope**: what problem, for whom, and why now.
2. **Goals and non-goals**: non-goals are as important; they stop scope creep and endless debate.
3. **The design**: APIs, data model, key flows, a diagram.
4. **Alternatives considered**: and why they lost. This is often the most valuable section for future readers.
5. **Cross-cutting concerns**: security, privacy, observability, migration, cost.

Keep it as short as the problem allows. A two-page doc that people actually read beats a 30-page doc that they skim. Once decided, record significant choices as Architecture Decision Records (covered in the architecture module) so the *why* outlives the meeting.

### The four kinds of documentation

The **Diátaxis** framework points out that documentation serves four different needs, and mixing them makes each worse:

| Kind | Reader wants to |
|---|---|
| Tutorial | Learn by doing |
| How-to guide | Achieve a specific task |
| Reference | Look up facts |
| Explanation | Understand why |

A README that mixes a walkthrough, exhaustive API details and a long architecture essay can make each task harder. A short overview can still link to those distinct resources. Separate them, and keep docs next to the code (**docs as code**) so they are reviewed and updated in the same pull request as the behaviour they describe.

**Runbooks** are a special case of how-to guide: step-by-step instructions for operational tasks and alerts. Every alert that can page someone should link to a runbook that says what it means, how to check impact and what to try first.

## Key takeaways
- Team communication and system boundaries influence each other; organisation alone does not guarantee independence.
- Raise the bus factor through collective code ownership, pairing, review and maintained documentation.
- Separate tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation; record goals, non-goals and alternatives in design docs.

## Further reading
- [Conway’s original observation](https://www.melconway.com/Home/Conways_Law.html)
- [Design Docs at Google — Malte Ubl](https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/)
- [Diátaxis documentation framework](https://diataxis.fr/)
- [Docs as Code — Write the Docs](https://www.writethedocs.org/guide/docs-as-code/)

questions.prompt: Only one engineer understands the billing reconciliation job. She is about to take three weeks of leave. What concept describes the risk, and what is the best longer-term response?

options.text: Technical debt; rewrite the job before she leaves
options.explanation: A rushed rewrite before she leaves adds risk and still leaves the knowledge in one head (hers, about the old version).

options.text: A bus factor of one; spread knowledge through pairing, a runbook and rotating ownership
options.explanation: Correct. The bus factor counts how many people would have to vanish before work stalls. Raising it means getting the knowledge into other heads and onto paper.

options.text: Conway's law; reorganise the team
options.explanation: Conway's law relates org structure to system structure. The problem here is concentrated knowledge, not team shape.

options.text: Alert fatigue; reduce the job's alerts
options.explanation: Alert volume is unrelated to how many people understand the job.

questions.workedExample:
1. Count the people who could keep the job running without help: one. The bus factor is one.
2. Short term: a handover session and a written runbook before the leave.
3. Longer term:
   - Pair on the next changes to the job.
   - Put a second person on its on-call rotation.
   - Document how it works and how to recover it.
4. The goal is that her leave, or her leaving, is a non-event.

questions.prompt: A README contains a getting-started walkthrough, a full list of configuration options, an essay on why the system uses event sourcing, and steps to rotate the database password. According to the Diátaxis framework, what is wrong?

options.text: Nothing; all documentation should be in one file
options.explanation: One file is not the issue. Mixing four kinds of documentation in one flow means each reader has to wade through material meant for someone else.

options.text: Configuration options should never be documented
options.explanation: Reference documentation for configuration is essential; it just belongs in a reference section.

options.text: Design rationale belongs only in code comments
options.explanation: Explanations of architecture are too broad for comments. They belong in explanation docs or ADRs.

options.text: It mixes a tutorial, reference material, an explanation and a how-to guide, which serve different needs and are better separated
options.explanation: Correct. A learner, someone looking up an option, someone wanting to understand a design choice and someone doing a task each need a differently shaped document.

questions.workedExample:
Map each part to a Diátaxis kind:

```
getting-started    tutorial
config options     reference
event sourcing     explanation
rotate password    how-to guide
```

Each has a different reader. Split them into separate pages (perhaps linked from a short README), so a tired on-call engineer looking for the password steps does not have to scroll past an essay.

questions.prompt: Your company has a monolith built by four teams. Every release needs all four to coordinate because their code is intertwined. Leadership wants independent services that teams can deploy separately. Which approach does Conway's law suggest?

options.text: Split the codebase into services first; team structure will adapt automatically
options.explanation: If the teams still communicate and work as one tangled group, the services tend to end up coupled too (a distributed monolith).

options.text: Merge all four teams into one large team to reduce coordination
options.explanation: Merging teams alone does not establish independent service ownership. Larger teams have more possible pairwise links, but actual communication overhead is not necessarily quadratic.

options.text: Add a release management team to coordinate the four
options.explanation: This adds a coordination layer rather than removing the need for coordination.

options.text: Organise each team around a business capability it owns end to end, and draw service boundaries to match those teams
options.explanation: Correct. Aligning responsibility and architectural boundaries can reduce unnecessary coordination, though interfaces, data ownership and deployment design still require engineering.

questions.workedExample:
1. Conway's law: system designs are influenced by the communication structure of the organisation that builds them.
2. Today the teams are entangled, and so is the code.
3. To get independent services, give each team independent ownership: a business capability (payments, catalogue, accounts) with its own code, data and deploy pipeline.
4. Draw the service boundaries along those team boundaries.
5. Use explicit interfaces and ownership agreements to reduce unnecessary cross-team dependencies; matching boxes on charts alone does not ensure independent deployment.

questions.prompt: A team is about to start a three-month project to replace its job scheduler. The tech lead suggests writing a design doc first. Which section is most likely to save the team from an expensive mistake, and why?

options.text: Goals, non-goals and alternatives considered, because they force agreement on scope and expose cheaper options before months of work are committed
options.explanation: Correct. Reviewers often spot that an existing tool meets the goals, or that a goal is not needed, while change costs only an edit to a document.

options.text: A detailed project timeline, because it keeps the team on schedule
options.explanation: A timeline is useful for planning, but it does not test whether the design itself is sound.

options.text: A list of class names, because it fixes the code structure early
options.explanation: Class details can matter when they explain a key interface or constraint, but a list of names alone does not establish scope or evaluate alternatives.

options.text: A glossary of terms, because it standardises vocabulary
options.explanation: Helpful for clarity, but it rarely changes the decision.

questions.workedExample:
1. The purpose of a design doc is to find mistakes while they are cheap: before code exists.
2. The most expensive mistakes are building the wrong thing or the hard version of the right thing.
3. **Goals and non-goals** pin down what must be true and what is explicitly out of scope.
4. **Alternatives considered** asks: could we use a managed scheduler, an existing open-source one, or extend the current one?
5. Reviewers challenging those sections may cut the project from three months to three weeks, or confirm the plan with much more confidence.

lessons.title: Review changes and build trust
lessons.summary: Keep code review focused on code health and create conditions for shared learning.
lessons.body:
Documentation spreads context before work starts; review spreads it as code changes. The same respect and willingness to ask questions matter in both.

## Code review
Code review catches defects, but its bigger benefits are spreading knowledge (raising the bus factor) and keeping the codebase consistent.

Google's published engineering practices give a useful standard: reviewers should favour approving a change once it **definitely improves the overall health of the code**, even if it is not perfect. Perfectionism in review slows everyone and drives people to accumulate changes into huge, unreviewable changes.

Practical habits:

- **Small changes.** Smaller coherent changes are easier to understand and review; line counts alone do not determine review quality. Split refactoring from behaviour change (see the refactoring lesson).
- **Fast responses.** Google's guide says one business day is the maximum time to respond to a review request. Slow reviews are a hidden tax on every engineer.
- **Comment on the code, not the person.** "This loop is O(n²); a set would make it O(n)" (where n is the number of items) rather than "why would you do this?".
- **Label severity.** Prefix optional suggestions with `Nit:` so the author knows what blocks approval.
- **Automate the trivial.** Formatters and linters in CI settle style, so humans spend review time on design and correctness.
- **Explain the why** in the PR description: context, approach, how it was tested, and what the reviewer should focus on.

## Team health in general
**Psychological safety** means the team believes it is safe to ask questions, acknowledge mistakes and take interpersonal risks. It helps people expose uncertainty during reviews and shared work.

- **Onboarding** is a test of your docs. Have every new joiner fix whatever confused them.
- **Pairing and mobbing** spread knowledge fast, especially on unfamiliar code.
- **Async by default** for things that do not need a meeting: written proposals, recorded decisions, threads rather than calls. Protect focus time.
- **Rotate ownership** of components and of on-call so expertise is not concentrated.

## Key takeaways
- Review small coherent changes promptly and distinguish blocking concerns from optional nits.
- Automate routine style so review can concentrate on design and correctness.
- Psychological safety, onboarding and shared work help people expose uncertainty and spread knowledge.

## Further reading
- [The Standard of Code Review — Google](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/standard.html)
- [Speed of Code Reviews — Google](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/speed.html)
- [Five dynamics of effective teams — Google](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/intl/en-emea/consumer-insights/consumer-trends/five-dynamics-effective-team/)

questions.prompt: A reviewer has been asked to look at a pull request that fixes a real bug and improves test coverage. It has two minor naming issues the reviewer would have done differently. According to Google's code review standard, what should the reviewer do?

options.text: Approve, leaving the naming suggestions as optional comments marked `Nit:`
options.explanation: Correct. Reviewers should favour approving a change once it definitely improves the overall code health, even if it is not perfect. Marking nits tells the author they are optional.

options.text: Block the PR until every name matches the reviewer's preference
options.explanation: Holding up a change that clearly improves code health over preferences is exactly what the standard warns against.

options.text: Approve without comment, since naming does not matter
options.explanation: Names do matter. The reviewer can still mention them, just without blocking.

options.text: Rewrite the PR themselves with better names
options.explanation: Taking over someone else's change removes their learning and ownership, and creates churn.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask: does this change improve the overall health of the code? It fixes a bug and adds tests: yes.
2. Are the remaining issues blocking (correctness, security, maintainability problems) or preferences? Preferences.
3. So approve, and record the suggestions as `Nit:` comments.
4. Result: the fix ships today, the author learns the reviewer's view, and nobody waits a week over two names.

questions.prompt: An engineer opens a 2,400-line pull request that refactors the persistence layer and adds a new feature. After four days it has one comment: "LGTM". What is the best lesson for next time?

options.text: Assign more reviewers to large PRs
options.explanation: Additional reviewers may help when responsibilities are clear, but do not remove the difficulty of a mixed, broad change.

options.text: Split it into small PRs, with the refactoring separate from the behaviour change, so each can be reviewed properly and quickly
options.explanation: Correct. Small changes get careful reviews and fast turnaround. Separating refactoring from behaviour change also makes it obvious which PR to examine if something breaks.

options.text: Skip code review for refactoring work
options.explanation: Refactorings can break things too. They should be reviewed, just separately and in small steps.

options.text: Ask the reviewer to spend a full day on it
options.explanation: Focused time can produce a thorough review, but splitting coherent changes reduces review complexity and waiting where practical.

questions.workedExample: Large mixed diffs increase the context a reviewer must track, but there is no universal maximum reviewable line count. Separate the persistence refactoring from the feature, then split caller migrations into coherent batches. Review each for behavior preservation, compatibility and tests; small size helps but does not guarantee quality or a one-day turnaround.

lessons.title: Design sustainable on-call
lessons.summary: Plan rotation capacity, actionable alerts, escalation and recovery for responders.
lessons.body:
Running a service includes supporting the people who respond when it fails. Staffing arithmetic is a starting constraint; sustainable workload requires explicit policies and regular review.

## On-call that people can sustain
If your team runs production services, someone needs to respond when they break at 3 a.m. Done badly, on-call burns people out and drives them away. Done well, it is a manageable part of the job that also teaches people how the system really behaves.

### Rotation design

Google's SRE book gives concrete guidelines worth knowing:

- No more than about **25%** of an engineer's time should be spent on call.
- With a primary and a secondary on call around the clock and week-long shifts, the ideal coverage calculation gives **eight engineers** for a single-site team, before leave and other resilience needs. Google separately recommends about **six per site** for dual-site teams, considering both coverage and critical team mass.
- Google reports around **6 hours** of work per incident in its experience, including diagnosis and follow-up, and uses at most **2 incidents per 12-hour shift** as a workload guideline. This is not a universal incident-duration estimate.
- Response expectations cited by Google: about **5 minutes** for user-facing, time-critical services, about **30 minutes** for less time-sensitive ones.

Where does eight come from? Two roles must be filled at every moment, and nobody may spend more than a quarter of their time in either of them:

```formula
E_min = R / f_max
E_min = 2 / 0.25
E_min = 8
where
E_min: the smallest team that can staff the rotation, in engineers
R: the number of on-call roles filled at all times: a primary and a secondary, so 2
f_max: the largest fraction of time one engineer may spend on call: 25%, which is 0.25
In words: two seats must always be filled and each person may sit in one only a quarter of the time, so you need four people per seat, eight in all.
```

With week-long shifts, each of the eight is on call (primary or secondary) for one week in every four, as the SRE book puts it. Real teams need more, to cover leave, illness and training.

The incident limit follows the same kind of reasoning:

```formula
H = k × t
H = 2 × 6 h = 12 h
where
H: the incident work generated during one shift, in hours (h)
k: the number of incidents in the shift; Google's guideline maximum is 2
t: the average hours of work per incident in Google's experience (root-cause analysis, remediation, and follow-up such as writing the postmortem and fixing bugs), about 6 h
h: hours
In words: two incidents of about six hours' work each fill a whole 12-hour shift, so more than two leaves no time to handle them properly.
```

A **follow-the-sun** rotation across suitable time zones and shift lengths can avoid night duty, with clear handovers. Check that the roster covers all 24 hours: London and San Francisco each working an ordinary eight-hour day do not provide complete coverage.

Other essentials:

- **A secondary** and a clear escalation path, so nobody is alone with a problem beyond them.
- **Handover notes** at the end of each shift: what fired, what is still open, what to watch.
- **Compensation and recovery**: pay or time off for on-call, and a lie-in after a bad night.
- **Training**: shadow shifts and practice incidents before someone carries the pager alone.

### Alert hygiene

The SRE book's test for a page: it should detect something **urgent, actionable and actively or imminently user-visible**. Every page should require human judgement; if a script could handle it, automate it.

Common failures and fixes:

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Pages on CPU > 80% without service risk | Tie pages to actionable current or imminent service risk |
| Same alert fires daily | Fix the cause; downgrade or remove only if paging is unnecessary |
| Alert with no runbook | Add a runbook; keep necessary service-risk detection |
| 20 alerts for 1 outage | Group and deduplicate |

**Alert fatigue** is dangerous: when most pages are noise, people stop treating them as urgent, and the real one gets missed. Review every page from the last rotation in a weekly meeting and ask "was this worth waking someone for?".

## Key takeaways
- Two simultaneous duty roles at a 25% duty fraction require at least eight people in the simplified single-site model.
- That arithmetic excludes leave and says nothing about incident volume or recovery needs.
- Page for urgent actionable threats to users and use runbooks, escalation and alert review.

## Further reading
- [Being On-Call — Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/being-on-call/)
- [Monitoring Distributed Systems — Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/)

questions.prompt: A team wants a 24/7 on-call rotation with a primary and a secondary at all times, week-long shifts, and no engineer on call more than 25% of the time. They are all in one office. What is the minimum team size? Ignore leave, illness, training and other unavailability; count primary and secondary duty together.

options.explanation: Four people covering two roles means each person is on call every other week, i.e. 50% of the time.
Correct. Two continuous roles each need four people if each person covers at most one quarter of the weeks. Eight people cover the ideal roster, before allowance for leave, sickness and training.
Two people could only staff primary and secondary by being on call permanently.
That would keep each person on call only 12.5% of the time; more than the 25% rule requires.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each week needs 2 on-call slots (primary and secondary).
2. Each engineer may fill at most 25% of weeks, i.e. 1 week in 4.

```formula
E_min = R / f_max
E_min = 2 / 0.25 = 8
where
E_min: the minimum number of engineers
R: on-call roles filled at all times, 2
f_max: the most time one engineer may be on call, 25% = 0.25
In words: two seats must always be filled and each person can sit in one only a quarter of the time, so you need four people per seat, eight in all.
```

3. Check: four weeks require eight role-weeks. Each person can cover one, so eight people are needed in this ideal roster.
4. So at least **8 engineers**, matching the figure in Google's SRE book.

questions.prompt: Which of these alerts should page an on-call engineer at 3 a.m.? Select all that apply.

options.text: Checkout errors have been above 5% for 10 minutes, breach the service paging policy and require intervention
options.explanation: Correct. It is urgent, user-visible and needs human action.

options.text: CPU on one of 40 stateless web servers is at 85%, with no current or imminent service risk
options.explanation: The stated busy node causes no current or imminent service risk, so it does not justify waking someone. Retain useful diagnostic measurements and investigate routine issues during working hours.

options.text: At the current rate, the primary database disk will fill in about 2 hours; automatic expansion is unavailable and an operator must act
options.explanation: Correct. Not yet user-visible, but imminently so, and someone has to act before it happens.

options.text: A nightly report finished 20 minutes later than usual but still met its delivery deadline
options.explanation: Mildly interesting, not urgent. It can be a ticket for working hours.

options.text: The log shipping agent restarted and fully recovered without data loss or backlog
options.explanation: It self-healed and needs no human. Paging on it trains people to ignore pages.

Apply the SRE book's test: is it **urgent**, **actionable**, and **actively or imminently user-visible**?

```
alert           urgent action user
checkout 5%     yes    yes    yes
1 node CPU      no     no     no
disk 2 hours    yes    yes    soon
late report     no     maybe  no
agent restart   no     no     no
```

Only A and C pass. The rest are dashboard or ticket material. Fewer, better pages are what keep a rotation sustainable.

questions.prompt: A team's on-call engineer received 31 pages last week; most were resolved by acknowledging and waiting. Two real outages were noticed late. Which changes would most improve the situation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review every page for urgency and actionability; remove or downgrade unnecessary pages while retaining needed service-risk detection
options.explanation: Correct. Review whether human action was actually necessary; downgrade or remove unnecessary pages while retaining important service-risk detection.

options.text: Align pages with actionable current or imminent user harm, using symptom-based alerts and justified predictive warnings rather than paging on every internal metric
options.explanation: Correct. Align pages with actionable current or imminent service symptoms; retain justified predictive alerts such as disk exhaustion.

options.text: Ensure every remaining paging alert links to a runbook
options.explanation: Correct. A runbook makes each page actionable and speeds up response, especially for less experienced engineers.

options.text: Tell the on-call engineer to respond faster
options.explanation: Investigate delayed detection and response. Noise is a plausible contributor; telling someone to respond faster does not address unnecessary pages.

options.text: Add more alerts so outages are less likely to be missed
options.explanation: Adding alerts indiscriminately increases noise. A targeted missing alert may still be appropriate if investigation establishes a detection gap.

questions.workedExample: Most pages needed no action, indicating poor paging signal. Investigate whether alert fatigue, missing detection, escalation or another cause explains the delayed outages. Google’s contextual guideline is at most two incidents per 12-hour shift, with a likely median of zero; multiple pages can refer to one incident. Remove or downgrade unnecessary pages, retain actionable service-risk alerts, group duplicates and provide runbooks.

lessons.title: Turn incidents into tracked improvements
lessons.summary: Write blameless incident reviews and make owned prevention work part of normal delivery.
lessons.body:
The on-call unit focused on response capacity. After a significant incident, use the evidence to improve both the service and the conditions in which people operate.

## Postmortems: learning, not blame
After a significant incident, the team writes a **postmortem**: what happened, the impact, the timeline, contributing factors and follow-up actions. The service-level mechanics (severity levels, incident command, SLO triggers) are in the System Design reliability module. What matters at team level is the culture around it.

A postmortem is **blameless**. It assumes everyone acted reasonably given what they knew at the time, and asks why the system made the mistake easy. "Alice ran the wrong migration" leads nowhere; "the migration tool runs against production by default with no confirmation" leads to a fix.

Blamelessness is not about being nice. It is practical: if people are punished for honest mistakes, they hide them, and the organisation stops learning. Amy Edmondson's research on **psychological safety** (a shared belief that it is safe to admit mistakes and take interpersonal risks) found an association with team learning (not a guarantee of causation in every team), and Google's internal Project Aristotle study of team effectiveness reported it as the most important factor of the five it identified.

What makes a postmortem worth writing:

- **Action items with owners and dates**, tracked like any other work. Untracked actions can create false confidence and leave preventable risks unaddressed.
- **Contributing factors, not a single root cause.** Real incidents usually involve several: a bug, a missing alert, a confusing dashboard.
- **Sharing.** Other teams learn from your failures cheaply. Many companies hold a regular postmortem review.

## Pitfalls
- **Hero culture.** Celebrating the person who fixes everything at 2 a.m. rewards the bus factor of one that caused the problem.
- **Docs written once and never updated.** Outdated instructions can mislead responders; flag uncertainty and maintain important procedures. Keep docs near the code and change them in the same PR.
- **Review as gatekeeping.** Blocking on style preferences, or leaving reviews for days, teaches people to avoid review.
- **Paging on causes rather than symptoms.** High CPU alone need not page, but imminent exhaustion that threatens users and requires urgent human action can justify a page.
- **Blameless in name only.** If a postmortem's real outcome is someone being quietly sidelined, the next incident will be reported later and less honestly.

## Key takeaways
- A blameless review explains decisions using the information available at the time.
- Record impact, timeline, contributing conditions and concrete preventive actions.
- Assign owners and track completion in the ordinary work system so the review changes practice.

## Further reading
- [Postmortem Culture — Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/)

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a postmortem to be **blameless**?

options.text: No one is allowed to mention who performed which action
options.explanation: Postmortems name actions and actors in the timeline. Blameless means not punishing them for reasonable actions, not hiding facts.

options.text: The incident is attributed to bad luck so nobody feels responsible
options.explanation: Blamelessness still looks for causes; it seeks them in systems and processes, not in luck.

options.text: It assumes people acted reasonably given what they knew, and looks for the conditions in the system that made the mistake possible or likely
options.explanation: Correct. The question becomes 'why did the system make this easy to do?', which leads to fixes like safer defaults, better tooling or clearer alerts.

options.text: Only managers write it, to protect the engineers involved
options.explanation: The people closest to the incident usually write it, because they know what happened.

questions.workedExample:
1. Contrast two findings:
   - 'Bob deleted the wrong table.' Outcome: Bob is careful for a while.
   - 'The admin tool connects to production by default and has no confirmation for destructive commands.' Outcome: a fix that protects everyone.
2. Blamelessness gets you the second kind, because people are honest when they are not punished for reasonable mistakes.
3. It does not remove accountability: the team is accountable for completing the action items.

questions.prompt: Six months after a postmortem, the same outage recurs. The postmortem listed five action items; none were completed because they sat in a separate document nobody tracked. What is the most important process change?

options.text: Write longer, more detailed postmortems
options.explanation: The analysis was not the problem. The follow-through was.

options.text: Identify the person responsible for the outage and require them to complete the actions
options.explanation: Assigning blame undermines honest reporting. Actions should be owned, but because they are work, not as punishment.

options.text: Track action items as normal tickets with owners and due dates in the team's backlog, and review their status regularly
options.explanation: Correct. Actions that live in the same system as all other work get prioritised, assigned and seen. Regular review (for example in a weekly ops meeting) catches ones that stall.

options.text: Stop writing postmortems for repeat incidents
options.explanation: A repeat incident is the strongest signal that learning has not stuck; it deserves more attention, not less.

questions.workedExample:
1. The postmortem identified fixes, so the learning happened on paper.
2. The failure is in follow-through: untracked items compete with nothing and lose to everything.
3. Put each action in the backlog as a ticket, with an owner, a priority and a due date.
4. Review open postmortem actions regularly. Some teams require top-priority actions to be done before the next feature work.
5. A postmortem with unfinished actions gives false comfort, which is arguably worse than none.
